captions.gbp:
Has your doctor ordered a scan with contrast? Here's what that means. Contrast is a helper, not a dye: it makes certain tissues and blood vessels show up more clearly, and it doesn't stain your organs. CT uses an iodine-based contrast and MRI uses gadolinium, usually given through a small IV; some CT scans use a drink instead. Your body clears it naturally, mostly in urine, and drinking extra water afterward helps. A brief warm feeling or metallic taste is normal and passes in minutes, and serious reactions are very uncommon. A seafood allergy doesn't raise your risk, and many scans, like most brain, spine and knee MRIs, don't need contrast at all. Before your scan, tell us about any past contrast reaction, allergies, diabetes, or kidney or thyroid disease, and whether you are pregnant, might be, or are breastfeeding.

Book online at advancedimg.com. General information, not medical advice. Sources: RadiologyInfo.org (ACR, RSNA); AAAAI.

alt_text.reel: Animated myth-or-fact quiz about contrast for medical scans, with upbeat music. Round 1: contrast dye stains your organs: myth, it's temporary and your body clears it, mostly in urine. Round 2: allergic to shellfish, no contrast for you: myth, it doesn't raise your risk, just tell us every allergy. Round 3: a warm flush with CT contrast is normal: fact, like a metallic taste, it fades in minutes. How many did you get? Drop your score in the comments. Questions? Just ask us.
alt_text.gbp: A smiling technologist beside a patient on an open MRI table. Need contrast for a scan? Here's what to know: it helps tissues show up clearly, and your body clears it naturally.

facts_checked: Contrast is not a dye that stains organs; iodine/barium for X-ray and CT, gadolinium for MRI; given by mouth or IV; warm flush and metallic taste with iodinated contrast lasting a few minutes; coolness at injection site with gadolinium; severe reactions very uncommon; eliminated in urine/stool, extra fluids help; tell staff about prior reactions, allergies, heart disease, diabetes, kidney disease, thyroid problems, pregnancy, breastfeeding: RadiologyInfo.org Contrast Materials (ACR/RSNA). Seafood allergy not a risk factor; 'iodine allergy' is a misnomer: AAAAI Radiocontrast and Seafood Allergy page. Most brain/spine/knee MRIs without contrast; prior CT-contrast reaction doesn't rule out gadolinium: amiweb services-data.ts FAQs. Checked 2026-10-20.
flag: Website CT page (services-data.ts ~lines 1084 and 1103): 'fast for 4 hours' before contrast and 'pause metformin for 48 hours' for everyone on it may be outdated; current ACR guidance does not require fasting for IV contrast and only asks to hold metformin for patients with eGFR under 30 or acute kidney injury. Not used in this post; worth checking with Milind.
